Welcome to your Danish citizenship exam companion.
This is Chapter Four, Denmark and the world, Episode One: the European Union.
Imagine Europe in the ruins after the Second World War.
The scale of international cooperation has grown ever since the end of that war, not least out of a strong wish to avoid new wars.
Future conflicts between countries were to be prevented.
Instead, countries should cooperate and find peaceful solutions.
Denmark takes part in this cooperation to a wide extent.
There has been, and still is, agreement among most of the parties in the Folketing that taking part mainly promotes Danish political and economic interests, and protects the country's security.
This has given Denmark influence on matters that reach beyond the country's borders.
But the decisions of these international organisations also help set the framework for Danish society.
International, and especially European, cooperation therefore has great importance for Denmark.
At the European level, it is especially the EU, the European Union.
Cooperation in the EU is particularly extensive and plays a big role for Denmark.
In addition, Denmark is, among other things, a member of the UN, NATO and the Council of Europe.
Denmark also cooperates with the other Nordic countries: Sweden, Norway, Finland and Iceland.
This takes place especially in the Nordic Council, Nordisk Råd, and the Nordic Council of Ministers, Nordisk Ministerråd.

The exams also ask this: the Nordic Council, Nordisk Råd, is the organisation for cooperation between the parliaments of the Nordic countries, and the Nordic Council of Ministers is the cooperation between the governments.
It is not called Nordtinget or the Nordic Union.
Now, the story of the European Union.
The first steps in its history were the European Coal and Steel Community, which was established in 1952 by six European countries.
Besides the wish to support peace and cooperation between the countries, one purpose was also to rebuild Europe economically and socially after the destruction of the war.
At the same time, the political world map had changed.
Europe was no longer the world's centre of power, and so the individual countries were to be strengthened by cooperating more.
A few years later, the six countries decided to go one step further.
In 1958, the Coal and Steel Community was expanded with the European Economic Community and the European Atomic Energy Community.
These three communities later became the European Communities, the EF.
The cooperation now became a broader economic cooperation.
Its purpose was especially to remove obstacles to trade between the countries, and thereby establish a more common market.
In 1993, the EU's internal market came into force.
This means that goods, services, persons and capital can move even more freely between the member countries than before.
The same year, the EF changed its name to the EU, the European Union.

The name change reflected that the cooperation, which until then had been cooperation on economic questions such as trade, agriculture and fisheries, was expanded with a broader range of political areas of cooperation.
Today, the EU consists of 27 member countries with a total of about 450 million inhabitants.
Here are the countries by the year they joined.
In 1958, the founding members: France, Germany, Italy, Belgium, the Netherlands and Luxembourg.
In 2004: Cyprus, the Czech Republic, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Hungary, Malta, Poland, Slovakia and Slovenia.
In addition, the United Kingdom joined the EU together with Denmark and Ireland in 1973, but left the cooperation again in 2020.
The EU's purpose is to solve common European problems.
The union is to strengthen cooperation in areas that are best handled by the EU's member countries together.

The EU's general objectives are to promote economic and social development, to strengthen Europe's role in the world, to strengthen the protection of European citizens' rights and interests, and to secure freedom, security and justice.
The EU countries cooperate today in almost all areas of society.
For example, an economic and monetary union has been established, the ØMU.
Under it, 20 member countries have a common currency, the euro.
EU cooperation also includes a common foreign and security policy.

In addition, there is police cooperation, cooperation on asylum and refugee policy, and the so-called Schengen cooperation, whose purpose is to create a common area without internal borders, but with a common external border.

The Schengen cooperation means that, as a starting point, the countries have removed personal checks at the borders within the Schengen area and made common visa rules for citizens from a number of countries outside the EU.
In the EU, the countries also cooperate on environmental protection, social conditions, employment, the labour market, education, regional development and foreign policy matters.
But there is a big difference in how extensive the cooperation is in the individual areas.
In some areas, common European legislation is drawn up.
In other areas, the EU is content to support the member countries' national policies.
In the EU cooperation, the member countries have given the EU some of the power that used to lie with the national parliaments and authorities.
Cooperation in the EU means that in some areas of law, EU legislation can be adopted that applies directly to citizens in the individual member country.
EU rules thus have the same effect as the country's own legislation.
Today many decisions in the EU are also made by so-called majority decisions.
That means a proposal can be adopted without all member countries agreeing.
A country can in other words be outvoted, but still be bound by the decision.
The EU is organised through a number of institutions that function independently of the member countries.
These are especially the European Commission, the European Parliament and the EU Court of Justice.
One example of an adopted EU law is the data protection regulation, most often called GDPR, the General Data Protection Regulation.
This law came into force in 2018 and sets requirements for how personal data is handled in the EU countries.

It has been of great importance for Danish companies and organisations, since there are new requirements for how and for how long they may store data about members and customers, as well as a requirement of consent when entering information about private persons.
A number of both public and private companies employ staff to make sure the companies' GDPR procedures are followed.
EU cooperation can also include matters that do not lead to actual EU legislation.
Instead, the aim is that the EU countries should learn from each other.
This can happen by the countries jointly formulating objectives for specific policy areas and then reporting on what they have done.
This is also called the open method of coordination.
The recommendations concern especially labour market policy, economic policy and social policy.
The member states have no duty to carry out the recommendations, but they often influence the member states' policy.
Here is your recap for Episode One.
The EU began with the Coal and Steel Community in 1952, with six countries.
In 1958 came the European Economic Community and the Atomic Energy Community, later the EF.
The internal market came into force in 1993, the same year the EF became the EU.
The EU has 27 member countries and about 450 million inhabitants.
The founding members in 1958 were France, Germany, Italy, Belgium, the Netherlands and Luxembourg.
Denmark and Ireland joined in 1973, together with the United Kingdom, which left in 2020.
Schengen means no internal border controls.
The institutions are the Commission, the Parliament and the Court of Justice.

This is Chapter Four, Episode Two: Denmark and the EU, and the Danish opt-outs.
What happens when Denmark hands some of its decision-making power to Brussels?
On certain areas, the EU has gained access to adopt legislation which the Folketing would otherwise adopt.
The EU has, for example, access to adopt rules that remove trade barriers between the member countries.
With its membership of the EU, Denmark has thus given up some of its right of self-determination.
The Danish constitution makes that possible.
But quite strict requirements are set for making such a decision.

At least five sixths, that is at least 150, of the Folketing's 179 members must say yes to Denmark's participation in the international cooperation, if it means Denmark gives up national self-determination.
If fewer than 150 members, but still a simple majority of 90, say yes, a referendum must be held on whether Denmark is to take part in the international cooperation.

Even though opinion polls show that the population is overwhelmingly positive about EU membership, it has often been divided in its attitude to whether the EU should cover more policy areas, and whether Denmark should abolish its EU opt-outs.
From the time the Danes said yes to membership of the EF in 1972, nine referendums have been held on changes in the cooperation.
Six times a majority of the voters have voted yes.
Three times a majority has voted no.
The Danes voted yes to membership of the EF in a referendum in 1972, and Denmark became a member in 1973.
Since the constitution of 1953, more referendums have been held about Denmark's relationship with the EU than about any other subject, more than about the constitution or the voting age.
That last point comes from what the exams ask, rather than from the textbook text.
Now, the Danish EU opt-outs, forbehold.
A crucial vote where the Danish population voted no was at the referendum on the Maastricht Treaty in 1992.
Denmark then got a special agreement with the other EU countries.
The special agreement is known as the Edinburgh Agreement.
It means that there are parts of the EU cooperation which Denmark does not take part in.
The agreement is also called "the four opt-outs".
The agreement was sent to a referendum the year after, in 1993.

This time a majority of Danes voted yes to the Maastricht Treaty with the following four EU opt-outs: union citizenship, the common currency, the euro, the defence area, and a common justice and immigration policy, the justice opt-out, retsforbeholdet.
The justice opt-out means that Denmark does not take part in cooperation in a number of legal areas, for example the common immigration and asylum policy and police work on cross-border crime.
In 2015 there was a referendum on whether the justice opt-out should be converted into an opt-in arrangement, a tilvalgsordning.

The opt-in arrangement would give Denmark the possibility of itself deciding which parts of the legal EU cooperation Denmark wants to take part in, but at the same time the possibility of choosing to stay outside other areas.
At the referendum in 2015, the Danes voted no to converting the justice opt-out.
Denmark therefore does not take part in the cooperation with the other EU countries in most legal areas, including the areas mentioned above.
The opt-out on the common currency means that Denmark is not obliged to introduce the euro.
In 2000 there was a referendum where the population was to decide whether they wanted to lift the opt-out and thereby introduce the euro in Denmark.
53.2 percent of Danes voted no to this proposal, and 46.8 percent voted yes.
Despite Denmark having a euro opt-out, Denmark still takes part in parts of the euro cooperation.

For example, Denmark follows a so-called fixed exchange rate policy, which means that the rate of the Danish krone follows the rate of the euro, so that you can always buy 1 euro for about 7.50 Danish kroner.
Likewise Denmark follows interest rate rises or cuts from the European Central Bank.
Previously Denmark also had an opt-out on the EU's defence and security policy, so Denmark, for example, did not take part in military operations that are part of the EU cooperation.
This so-called defence opt-out was lifted as a result of a referendum on the first of June, 2022.
A majority of 66.9 percent voted yes to lifting the opt-out, while a minority of 33.1 percent voted no.
So today Denmark has no defence opt-out, and does take part in the EU's defence and security policy.
Denmark's opt-out on union citizenship was introduced to guarantee that union citizenship should not develop into something on a par with national citizenship or completely replace it.
With the Amsterdam Treaty coming into force in 1999, this came to apply to all member countries.
Therefore this Danish EU opt-out is also no longer relevant.
So of the four opt-outs from 1993, two still apply: the euro opt-out, and the justice opt-out.
The defence opt-out was abolished in 2022, and the union citizenship opt-out is no longer relevant.
Here is your recap for Episode Two.
To give up national self-determination, at least 150 of the 179 members of the Folketing must say yes; if fewer than 150, but at least 90, say yes, there must be a referendum.
Since 1972, nine referendums on changes to the cooperation: six yes, three no.
In 1992, Denmark voted no to the Maastricht Treaty, which led to the Edinburgh Agreement and the four opt-outs.
In 1993, Denmark voted yes with the opt-outs.
The four were union citizenship, the euro, defence, and justice.
In 2000, 53.2 percent voted no to the euro.
About 7.50 kroner buys one euro, the fixed exchange rate.
In 2015, Denmark voted no to converting the justice opt-out.
On the first of June, 2022, 66.9 percent voted yes to abolishing the defence opt-out.
Union citizenship is no longer relevant since 1999.
Two opt-outs still apply: the euro and justice.
Warning: older exams asked about a Danish defence opt-out.
That was true until the first of June 2022, so if an option says defence, it is outdated.
And the exams also ask this: Greenland and the Faroe Islands are part of the Danish Realm, but they are not part of the EU.

This is Chapter Four, Episode Three: the EU's institutions, and the Council of Europe.
Who actually makes the decisions in the EU?
The most important EU institutions are: one, the European Commission.
Three, the European Council, also called the EU summits.
Four, the Council of the European Union, in short the Council or the Council of Ministers.
And five, the EU Court of Justice.
The short version is that it is the main rule that the European Commission puts forward proposals for new EU legislation.
It is then the Council and the European Parliament that jointly adopt, change or reject the proposal.
Denmark is represented in the EU in different ways in these institutions.
Like the other member countries in the EU, Denmark sends one commissioner to the European Commission.
The European Commission today has 27 members.
The Commission is to come up with concrete proposals for new legislation.
It must also take other initiatives that can put the overall political objectives of the treaties and the EU summits into effect.
The European Commission has both the right and the duty to propose new legislation to carry out EU policy.
The European Commission also checks whether the member countries comply with EU legislation.
If a country does not, the Commission can bring a case against that country at the EU Court of Justice.
The individual members of the Commission are appointed by the individual member countries for a five-year period and must function independently of the member countries they come from.
That means they are only to work for the EU's interests and not for that member country.
Like the Danish ministers, they have responsibility for each their own area.

For example, there is a commissioner for the economy and productivity, a commissioner for climate, a commissioner for agriculture and food, a commissioner for defence and space, a commissioner for fisheries and oceans, and so on.
Denmark's EU commissioner has since 2024 been Dan Jørgensen, born 1975, from the Social Democrats, who was previously a member of the European Parliament and climate minister in Denmark.
He is commissioner for energy and housing.
If an older exam asks who the Danish commissioner is, the answer used to be Margrethe Vestager; today it is Dan Jørgensen.
In the period 2014 to 24, Margrethe Vestager, born 1968, from the Social Liberal Party, who was earlier minister for economic and interior affairs in Denmark, was appointed as Danish commissioner.
Margrethe Vestager was vice president of the Commission and commissioner for competition policy in the EU.
To help propose and carry out EU legislation, the EU commissioners have a large administration, which resembles the Danish ministries.
In the EU they are called directorates-general.
The European Parliament is the directly elected assembly in the European cooperation, since its members are elected by the citizens of the EU's member countries.
The European Parliament functions overall as a kind of legislative authority in the EU.
It resembles the Danish Folketing, but has more limited power.
For example, the European Parliament cannot levy tax.
The European Parliament adopts new legislation on the basis of proposals from the European Commission.
In addition, the European Parliament must among other things also adopt the EU's expenditure budget.
The European Parliament consists of 720 members from the 27 EU countries.
Each country has a number of seats that reflects the country's population.
Denmark has 15 members in the European Parliament, while big countries like Germany, France and Italy have a larger number of members.
Elections to the European Parliament are held every five years.
The members of the European Parliament are grouped in parties or groups on the basis of their political views, and not by which country they come from.
The Danish members of the European Parliament are therefore spread across a conservative group, a social democratic group, a liberal group, a green group and other groups.
The latest election to the European Parliament was held in June 2024.
As a result, the 15 Danish members are distributed among the following parties: the Socialist People's Party, SF, 3.
The Alternative also stood in the election, but did not get enough votes to be elected.
Third, the European Council, the EU summits.
The Danish prime minister meets with the other heads of government in the EU at EU summits in the European Council.
Here the leaders lay down the overall political framework for the cooperation in the EU.
They also make decisions on other important political questions.
That can for example be about the EU's enlargement, the EU's treaties or the EU's policy on the global stage.
Decisions are, as a main rule, made by consensus.
Fourth, the Council, the Council of the European Union, in Danish Rådet for Den Europæiske Union, or Ministerrådet.
In the Council, the member states' ministers from the member countries' governments meet at regular intervals.
That is why this institution is also often called the Council of Ministers.
The Council thus in practice consists of changing sector ministers, one from each country.
When, for example, something concerning the environment is to be discussed and adopted, it is the 27 environment ministers who meet.
If it concerns the internal market, the business ministers meet.
And if a proposal for EU legislation concerning agriculture is on the agenda, the food ministers meet.
The Council legislates together with the European Parliament.
That means adoption of EU legislation as a starting point requires support from both the Council and the European Parliament.
In a few areas, however, the European Parliament must only be consulted, while it is the Council that makes the final decision.
The different countries in the EU also take turns holding a so-called presidency.
This goes in turns every six months, and the country that has the EU presidency leads the meetings of the Council and a long series of committees.
The last Danish EU presidency was in 2025.
Do not confuse this with Denmark's seat on the UN Security Council in 2025 to 26, which is a seat, not a presidency.
Fifth, the EU Court of Justice.
Like the other countries in the EU, Denmark has one judge in the Court of Justice of the European Union, in everyday speech often called the EU Court.
The EU Court's task is to ensure that EU legislation is complied with.
The court can, among other things, settle conflicts between two member countries, and between the EU and the individual member country.
The EU Court can also decide how the EU rules are to be understood.
If a national court in a member country is in doubt about that, it can ask the EU Court.
Now, a very different organisation with a confusingly similar name: the Council of Europe.
Denmark has been a member of the Council of Europe since it was established in 1949.
In 1949, the Council of Europe consisted of ten Western European democracies.
The Council of Europe is not an EU institution.
It is an independent organisation in Europe.
The Council of Europe is thus a completely different institution from the European Council.
Before a country can become a member of the Council of Europe, it must recognise its citizens' personal and political rights of freedom.
The purpose of the Council of Europe is to ensure close cooperation between its member countries in a long list of political areas.
The aim is also to develop European democracy.
Russia was suspended from the Council of Europe after the attack on Ukraine in 2022.
The Council of Europe is, among other things, behind the drawing up of the European Convention on Human Rights from 1950.
It has also set up a court in the area of human rights, the European Court of Human Rights, which is to ensure that the convention is complied with.
By acceding to the convention, Denmark has committed itself to comply with the fundamental freedoms and human rights.
That means, among other things, freedom of expression, assembly and religion.
In 1992, the Convention on Human Rights was formally incorporated into Danish law.
It thereby stands on a par with other laws in Denmark, but below the constitution.
Denmark has at the same time recognised that individuals, under certain conditions, can bring a case against Denmark before the European Court of Human Rights.
Here is your recap for Episode Three.

There are five EU institutions, in Danish Europa-Kommissionen, Europa-Parlamentet, Det Europæiske Råd, Rådet for Den Europæiske Union, and EU-Domstolen: the Commission, the Parliament, the European Council, the Council of Ministers, and the Court of Justice.
The Commission proposes legislation; the Council and the Parliament adopt it.
The Commission has 27 members, one per country, appointed for five years.
Denmark's commissioner since 2024 is Dan Jørgensen, for energy and housing; Margrethe Vestager was commissioner 2014 to 24.
The Parliament has 720 members, 15 from Denmark, elected every five years; the latest election was in June 2024.
The European Council is the heads of government, deciding by consensus.
The Council presidency changes every six months; the last Danish presidency was in 2025.
Denmark has one judge in the EU Court.

The Council of Europe is not an EU institution: Denmark has been a member since 1949, there are 47 members, and it produced the European Convention on Human Rights of 1950, which became part of Danish law in 1992.

This is Chapter Four, Episode Four: the United Nations, and Denmark's global cooperation.
Denmark's international relations do not stop at Europe.
Denmark is also a member of many organisations that deal with larger regional or global questions.
One of the most important is the UN.
Denmark also has a large cooperation on development with a number of developing countries in, among other places, Africa, Latin America and Asia.
The UN, the United Nations, Forenede Nationer, FN in Danish, is a worldwide organisation which consists of independent states.
The UN was founded in 1945, shortly after the end of the Second World War.
From the start, the UN had the support of 51 states.
Today the number of members is 193.
Denmark has been a member of the UN since its foundation in 1945.
The UN's most important tasks lie within peace and security, human rights, development activities and humanitarian efforts.
Questions such as conflicts, economy, poverty, hunger, diseases and the environment are therefore central to the UN's work.
In addition, the UN works with children's conditions, women's rights, culture and education.
The UN's headquarters is in New York, but some of its sub-organisations have their headquarters elsewhere in the world, among others in Geneva, Nairobi and Vienna.
The highest leader in the UN is the UN Secretary-General.
The UN holds an annual General Assembly, which takes place at the UN's headquarters in New York.
The General Assembly has many purposes, including discussing current matters in the UN's member countries, adopting the UN's budget, and discussing reports from the UN Security Council.
The main task of the UN Security Council is to deal with conflicts that may threaten international peace and security.
The Security Council has five permanent members.
They are Russia, China, the United Kingdom, the USA and France, which were the five most important countries that helped win the Second World War.
One idea behind this composition was also that wars and conflicts could be avoided by dialogue and cooperation between the then five most significant powers.
The Security Council has ten other member countries.
They are selected by the General Assembly for two years at a time.
Denmark is a member of the Security Council in the period 2025 to 26, and has previously been a member in the periods 1967 to 68, 1985 to 86 and 2005 to 06.
The five permanent members have a veto.
That means that if just one of these countries votes against a decision, it cannot be carried out.
As the countries often have different and conflicting interests, it is often difficult to adopt significant decisions.
Since 1946, the veto has been used 329 times, most often by the Soviet Union and Russia, and the USA.
For example, Russia has in recent years used its veto to block the Security Council from condemning Russia's invasion of Ukraine.
And the USA has, because of its close relationship with Israel, among other things used its veto to prevent the UN from condemning new Israeli settlements in the Palestinian areas.

Another criticism of the UN system is that the global balance of power has changed since 1945, because some of the Security Council's permanent members have lost power and significance in the meantime.
The USA is still regarded as the world's strongest power and China as the second strongest.
But many would say that the Security Council's three European members, Russia, France and the United Kingdom, are no longer global great powers.
In addition, for example neither India, with the world's largest population, nor any countries from Africa or South America, are represented among the permanent members.
In Copenhagen lies the so-called UN City, FN-byen, where more than 1,500 people of more than 100 different nationalities work.
The UN City houses 11 UN organisations, including the World Health Organization, WHO, the UN High Commissioner for Refugees, UNHCR, and the UN's organisation to help children, UNICEF.

UNICEF's world warehouse in Copenhagen contains, among other things, medical supplies, school equipment, products to turn dirty water into drinking water and much more, which is sent out to millions of children all over the world.
The UN's 17 Sustainable Development Goals, verdensmål.

The UN's member countries adopted, at a summit in New York in September 2015, the new goals for sustainable development, which form the framework for the global development effort up to the year 2030.
The 17 goals apply to all the world's countries, and thereby also Denmark.
The 17 goals are very ambitious and cover a wide range.
Besides fighting poverty and social development, the goals also focus on economic and environmental development, equality, climate, and include goals for peace and security.

With the goals, the UN's member countries have thus, among other things, committed themselves to abolishing extreme poverty, securing education for all, better health, decent jobs and sustainable growth in all countries.
The 17 goals are: Goal 1, no poverty.
Goal 8, decent jobs and economic growth.
Goal 11, sustainable cities and local communities.
Goal 16, peace, justice and strong institutions.

The exams also ask about one more UN agreement: in 2015 the UN adopted the Paris Agreement, the climate agreement in which Denmark and many other countries have committed to reducing greenhouse gas emissions.
That fact is not in the textbook chapter itself.
Here is your recap for Episode Four.
The UN was founded in 1945, with 51 states; today it has 193 members.
Denmark has been a member since 1945.
The headquarters is in New York.
The Security Council has five permanent members, Russia, China, the United Kingdom, the USA and France, with a veto, used 329 times since 1946.
It also has ten other members, elected for two years; Denmark is a member in 2025 to 26, and was earlier in 1967 to 68, 1985 to 86 and 2005 to 06.
The UN City in Copenhagen has more than 1,500 employees, over 100 nationalities and 11 UN organisations, including WHO, UNHCR and UNICEF.
The 17 Sustainable Development Goals were adopted in September 2015 and run until 2030.

This is Chapter Four, Episode Five: development cooperation, and the focus on Africa.
Denmark gives financial support to many of the world's poorest countries.
This support is called international development cooperation.
Denmark is one of a few countries in the world that meet the UN's target that countries should give 0.7 percent of gross national income, GNI, in development aid.
In 2026, that corresponds to about 23 billion kroner.

The aims of Danish aid are, for example, to fight poverty, create jobs, trade and investment, help with the green transition, fight corruption, promote democracy and human rights, and women's and girls' rights.
Some of the Danish development aid is given as direct aid to the developing countries.
Denmark gives, for example, money directly to the developing countries, to humanitarian work, and to the work carried out by civil society organisations.
Denmark also gives aid in the form of contributions to international organisations such as the EU, the UN and the World Bank.
Part of the money in 2026 is also given to help Ukraine with humanitarian aid and the rebuilding of the country.
Since 1971, Danida has been responsible for Danish development policy.
Danida is an independent department under the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.
At the Danish embassies and representations abroad there are both local and Danish dispatched staff who handle the development cooperation with the individual country.
Africa is the part of the world that has historically had the biggest focus in Danish development policy, and which has received most of the Danish development aid.
That is connected, among other things, with Africa being a neighbour to Europe, and with what happens in Africa being able to have great importance for Europe, and thereby for Denmark.
There is a big difference between the 54 African countries, but overall Africa is the world's poorest continent, and in several places there are civil wars and other conflicts.
And the population is growing fast, and with it Africa's importance.
Africa's population has almost doubled over the last 25 years, from 835 million in 2001 to 1.6 billion in 2026.
Towards 2050, according to the UN, a further population increase of almost 1 billion is expected, to a total of 2.5 billion.

That creates on the one hand the opportunity for more economic growth, more trade and more investment, but also increases the risk of bigger problems with climate change and poverty, which can also lead to more people fleeing or migrating, and some towards Europe via the life-threatening routes across the Mediterranean.
In 2024, about 130,000 illegal arrivals from Africa to Europe were registered.
The average African emits far fewer of the greenhouse gases that are the main cause of climate change than, for example, the average American, Chinese or European.
But Africa's emissions are expected to grow in the coming decades.
And in any case it is in Africa that some of the worst consequences of climate change are felt, in the form of, for example, floods, extreme heat, failed harvests and more areas with desert.
A closer cooperation between the European and African countries is therefore meant to ensure, among other things, that Europe becomes the preferred partner and does not lose political influence.
The Danish government presented in 2024 a new and comprehensive "Strategy for a strengthened Danish engagement with the African countries".
It proposes that Denmark engages more in Africa and also focuses on creating equal partnerships with the African countries.

The strategy continues the support, while focusing on peace and security, the fight against climate change, and better opportunities for investment in African countries, economic growth and more trade with Danish companies.
Other aims are also to create more exchange of culture and education, and to reduce the number of illegal migrants towards Europe.
Here is your recap for Episode Five.
Denmark meets the UN's target of 0.7 percent of gross national income in development aid, which in 2026 is about 23 billion kroner.
Danida has been responsible for Danish development policy since 1971, as a department under the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.
Africa is the continent with the biggest focus.
The population grew from 835 million in 2001 to 1.6 billion in 2026, and is expected to reach 2.5 billion by 2050.
About 130,000 illegal arrivals from Africa to Europe were registered in 2024.
In 2024, the government presented a new strategy for a strengthened Danish engagement with the African countries.

This is Chapter Four, Episode Six: Danish foreign and security policy after the Cold War.
Even though Denmark, with its entry into NATO in 1949, gave up its traditional neutrality, Denmark kept a relatively low military profile until the end of the Cold War, around 1990.
Denmark did, however, take part in many of the UN's peacekeeping missions.
The task here was typically partly to help ensure that a ceasefire was observed, and partly to protect the civilian population.
Now the period of foreign policy activism after the Cold War, 1990 to 2022.
After the end of the Cold War, NATO's goals gradually changed.
NATO is an international defence alliance, a forsvarsalliance, not a trade area and not a refugee cooperation.
But the goal also increasingly became to promote peace, democracy, human rights and the rule of law around the world.
In that connection it played a big role that NATO, after the end of the Cold War, has been clearly the world's strongest military and security-policy alliance.
NATO, led by the USA, was thus less worried about being attacked or ending up in armed conflict with other countries.
And Denmark developed, little by little, a so-called "activist foreign policy".
That meant that Denmark began to take part more actively in international conflicts that went beyond peacekeeping missions.
This was expressed in different ways.
In 1990 to 91, Iraq occupied its neighbour Kuwait.
On the basis of a UN decision, the USA led a military effort to liberate Kuwait.
Denmark sent a warship as a contribution to the international military force.
The ship did not take part in active combat, but had the task of enforcing the international community's trade blockade against Iraq.
In connection with the civil war in Yugoslavia in the beginning of the 1990s, Danish soldiers were sent out as part of the UN forces.
Here they were involved in direct combat with Serbian forces in Bosnia in 1994.
Also in Kosovo, which at that time was a province in Serbia, there was civil war at the end of the 1990s.
Here the Albanian population majority was subjected to abuses from the Serbian government.
After long negotiations without result, NATO intervened militarily in 1999.
Danish fighter planes took part in NATO's actions.
Next, the efforts after the terror attack on the USA in 2001.
A turning point for security policy in the NATO alliance, and Denmark among them, was the terror attack on the USA on the eleventh of September, 2001.
Here terrorists killed about 3,000 people by hijacking passenger planes and flying them into, among other things, the World Trade Center in New York.
After this terror attack, fighting terrorism became an important task for the alliance.
After the terror attack, NATO took a new step and decided to strengthen its ability to fight any threat against the populations, territories and military forces of the member countries.
This also applied to terror threats from terror groups.
Denmark has therefore since 2001 taken part in military missions around the world that have had a focus on these goals.
The terror organisation Al Qaeda, which was behind the attack on the USA on the eleventh of September, 2001, had its base in Afghanistan.
This gave occasion for forces, led by NATO and with a mandate from the UN, to invade the country in October 2001 and depose the Islamist Taliban government, which cooperated with Al Qaeda.
In 2002, a large majority in the Danish Folketing decided to send Danish soldiers to Afghanistan to take part in the war.
For 20 years, the Taliban fought a guerrilla war against the international forces and the new, Western-supported Afghan government.
The Danish soldiers were, among other things, stationed together with British troops in the southern Helmand province, which was one of the most unsettled in the country.
In total 44 Danish soldiers lost their lives during the fighting.

After 2014, the task of the Danish deployed soldiers was to train and support the Afghans so they themselves could take care of security in the country, and since then the Danish and other countries' soldiers have been withdrawn completely.
As the international forces left Afghanistan, the country's government and army collapsed.
In August 2021, the Taliban recaptured the capital Kabul and thereby power in the country.
The West, including Denmark, started a historically extensive evacuation of its own diplomats, military advisers, and of Afghans who had worked for the West, such as interpreters, during the war.
In 2003, the USA and a number of other countries fought a war against Iraq and the country's dictator Saddam Hussein.
The war was justified by Iraq not living up to its obligations on military disarmament, which had been imposed on it by the UN after the Gulf War in 1991.
In addition, the USA believed that Iraq had illegally developed weapons of mass destruction.
However, no such weapons of mass destruction were ever found.
This war was without a clear mandate from the UN, and it was not a NATO mission either.
The war was carried out by an alliance of countries led by the USA and with the support of, among others, the United Kingdom and Denmark.
Several NATO members, among them Germany, France and Norway, did not want to support the war.
In Denmark it was only a small majority in the Folketing that voted for Denmark's participation in the Iraq War.
Saddam Hussein was removed from power in 2003.
After that the focus shifted to rebuilding Iraq after the war, to creating better living conditions for the Iraqis through humanitarian efforts, and to creating democracy.
The Danish soldiers took part in this work together with soldiers from other countries.

This work has, however, been made difficult by the removal of Saddam Hussein setting off a flare-up of several conflicts in Iraq between the country's different ethnic and religious groups, including the Sunni Muslim minority, which Saddam Hussein came from, and the Shia Muslim majority, which now gained power.
At times the situation in Iraq has resembled civil war.
In total, eight Danish soldiers died in connection with the American-led intervention in Iraq.
In 2011, an uprising broke out against Libya's dictator Muammar al-Gaddafi.
The uprising happened at the same time as uprisings in several neighbouring countries, for example Tunisia, Egypt and Syria, which became known as "the Arab Spring".
A united Folketing decided that Denmark could take part in a military intervention in Libya.
The intervention was, in accordance with a mandate from the UN, to protect the civilian population from abuses by Gaddafi.
Denmark provided aircraft for the operation and carried out several bombings of Gaddafi's army and military bases.
Subsequently Libya has been an extremely unstable country with weak governments, and where warring groups have been in something that is best described as a civil war.
Libya has also become the starting point for many African migrants who seek to Europe across the Mediterranean.

The story now turns back home.
In recent years, the USA and its allies have again turned their gaze away from promoting peace, democracy, human rights and the rule of law around the world through military actions.

That is due, among other things, to the limited success of the operations in, for example, Iraq, Afghanistan and Libya, where in the long run it did not succeed to achieve the goals of creating peace and setting up democratic governments that support the West.
And not least significant, there is again much greater focus on a solid and effective territorial defence.
That is the ability to defend your own territory against an attack from other countries.
This is due to a number of different circumstances.

Decisive for the wish to strengthen the European NATO countries' territorial defence has been that the relationship between the West and Russia has been marked by more and more conflicts in recent years.

Russia has expressed that it feels its interests are violated, because most of Russia's neighbouring countries in Central and Eastern Europe, which were allied with Russia, the Soviet Union, during the Cold War, have since 1999 been admitted as members of NATO.
Also three countries in the former Soviet Union, Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania, have joined NATO.
Conversely, NATO has emphasised that the countries are free to apply for admission to the defence alliance.
In addition, the Warsaw Pact and the Soviet Union were dissolved, in 1991, with Russia's own acceptance.
The increased tensions have great importance for Denmark's security-policy situation.
That is not least because Denmark is located by the Baltic Sea, which both NATO and Russia regard as an important area of interest.
Russia has, among other things, threatened to attack the three Baltic countries Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania.
And the Danish Defence Intelligence Service assesses, for example, that it is very likely that Russia is behind disturbance of navigation signals, GPS, over the Baltic Sea.
Since 2014, Russia has kept the peninsula of Crimea in Ukraine occupied, and Russia has also sent weapons and soldiers to support pro-Russian rebels' fight to break away parts of eastern Ukraine.

Last but not least, Russia in February 2022 launched an extensive military attack on Ukraine, which has led to war between the Russian and Ukrainian armies and thereby great destruction and sent millions of Ukrainians fleeing.
In response, the West, including Denmark, has supported Ukraine with weapons, training and money to defend itself against the Russian attacks.
In this context, Denmark is one of the countries in the world that have helped Ukraine the most, and especially in relation to the size of Denmark's population.
Among other things, the Danish government decided in 2023 to donate 19 F-16 fighter jets to Ukraine and train pilots from the Ukrainian air force to use the planes.

Further, the West has tried to weaken the Russian economy with extensive economic sanctions, with exclusion of Russian banks from the international payment system SWIFT, a ban on selling a number of goods to Russia, and a decision to stop buying Russian oil.
Many Western companies have withdrawn from Russia.
Another reason for the rearmament is that the USA has been dissatisfied that most European NATO countries let their defence budgets fall quite a lot after the end of the Cold War.
The USA therefore believes that Europeans have left too large a part of the bill for Europe's own security to the USA, which spent far more money on defence.
Therefore, the NATO countries agreed in 2014 that each country should spend two percent of their gross domestic product, the value of a country's total production, on defence.
And the ambitions have grown since.
In June 2025, the target has been raised to five percent.

Denmark has on the one hand been one of the NATO countries that after the Cold War has been most willing to send soldiers to American-led military operations abroad, for example in Afghanistan and Iraq.
But on the other hand, Denmark spent less money on defence.
For example, Denmark's defence budget fell in the period 1990 to 2015 from 2.0 to 1.05 percent of gross domestic product, far below NATO's target of two percent.
And the number of conscripts fell in the same period from about 10,500 to 4,300 a year.
Furthermore, the money for defence was increasingly spent on being able to send forces out on international tasks rather than defending Denmark.
This led to a clear reduction in the number of soldiers, and many of the defence's barracks, naval stations and air stations were closed down.
In addition, US foreign policy seems to be changing.
Among other things because China's power is growing, and the USA is thereby increasingly prioritising countering the competition from China.
This happens, among other things, by moving more investment and more military to Asia and the Pacific and to the USA's own neighbouring area.
It creates uncertainty about the extent to which the USA will continue to take part in the defence of Europe, not least against a possible attack from Russia.

As a result of the war in Ukraine, NATO's increased targets, and the changed priorities in American foreign policy, Denmark and the other European countries have decided that far more money is to be spent on defence in future, so that we get better at defending ourselves in case of an attack.
The Danish defence spending already in 2024 reached over two percent of gross domestic product.
This now applies to all 32 member countries of NATO.
Together, the European NATO countries have increased defence spending from 1.4 percent of gross domestic product in 2014 to about 2.3 percent in 2025.
And very large additional amounts have been set aside in the coming years, which in 2026 are expected to lift Denmark's defence spending to 3.5 percent.
In the same period, US defence spending has fallen from 3.7 to 3.2 percent of GDP.
Thus the difference between the American and the European defence spending, in relation to the size of the economies, has become considerably smaller.

The increased funding is to be used, among other things, to buy more and newer equipment, such as more tanks and fighter jets, as well as underwater torpedoes and advanced defence systems that can shoot down enemy aircraft and missiles from the ground.

In addition, it was decided in 2024 that more soldiers are to be called up, so that the number of conscripts is to be increased to 7,500, from about 5,200 in 2023, and that the service time for most is extended from four to 11 months.
Now to the Realm Community, Greenland and the Arctic in Danish foreign policy.
Greenland, which is part of the Danish Realm Community, had a special importance during the Cold War.
Greenland lies close to both the USA and the then Soviet Union.
In most cases you had to fly over Greenland to take the shortest route between the USA, Europe and the Soviet Union.
The shortest way for rockets in case of war between the USA and Russia, the Soviet Union, also goes over Greenland.
That gave the island great strategic importance in relation to defence cooperation.
In 1951, Denmark and the USA signed an agreement about the USA's military activities in Greenland.
The same year, the Americans began building a large air base at Qaanaaq, Thule, in northern Greenland.
On the base, the USA also built a radar station that could monitor the airspace over Greenland and the waters around Greenland.
The base was central to the air defence of the USA and NATO, and it is still used today by the USA, under the name Pituffik Space Base.
The warmer climate and the melting of the ice in and around Greenland have increased the country's strategic importance in recent years.
In Qaanaaq, near the base, lies the world's northernmost deep-water port, where the water is deep enough for large ships to dock.

And with the warmer climate and the melting of the ice, it is increasingly possible to extract natural resources such as rare earths, uranium, oil, gas and minerals in Greenland that have until now been frozen.
If the sea in the Arctic in future becomes relatively ice-free in summer, it also opens for new, shorter shipping routes via the Arctic Ocean between the world's continents.
The Arctic area has therefore, via Greenland, again come far more into the centre of Danish security policy.
The great powers the USA, Russia and China are all interested in the areas of the Arctic in different ways.
This means the Arctic is increasingly marked by a tense relationship between these countries.

It is both about the countries having an interest in protecting themselves against attack from others, and about the countries having growing economic interests in, for example, mining and transport of goods by ship.
The Danish inspection ship Vædderen patrols off the coast of Greenland.
In recent years, the American president Donald Trump, born 1946, has expressed a wish that Greenland should become part of the USA.
This wish has, however, been rejected by both the Greenlandic and the Danish government.
In the Ilulissat Declaration from 2008, five Arctic states, Denmark and Greenland, Norway, the USA, Canada and Russia, have declared that they agree to cooperate on peaceful relations in the Arctic.
But the declaration was drawn up in a completely different international situation from today, since the relationship between some of the countries has become more tense since 2008.
To strengthen cooperation on sustainable development in the Arctic areas within, among other things, environment, climate, health and shipping, the Arctic Council was established in 1996.
The council has participation by the countries that have territories in the Arctic regions.
That is the USA, Canada, Russia and the five Nordic countries.
In addition, six organisations take part, each representing the indigenous peoples, including the Inuit Circumpolar Council, ICC.
Greenland and the Faroe Islands have a strong independent voice in the Arctic Council.
Greenland has a leading role in the Kingdom's current chairmanship of the Arctic Council, 2025 to 2027.
